newsitem.title: JAPAN: Rubber-prices seen steady, shrugging off INRO news.
newsitem.headline: Rubber-prices seen steady, shrugging off INRO news.

text.p: Japanese rubber futures markets are likely to be steady this week, ignoring the news that the International Natural Rubber Organisation (INRO) has raised its buffer stock reference price, traders said on Monday.
INRO said on Friday it had raised its buffer stock reference price by four percent to 214.95 Malaysian/Singapore cents a kg to reflect an increase in world rubber prices.
The reference price is basically a neutral level where INRO's buffer stock manager does not intervene to buy or sell rubber in the market.

"The news that INRO raised its reference price will have little impact on the rubber markets, as they have already discounted that as a factor," said Nobufumi Iimori, manager of the Commodities Investment Division of Nihon Unicom Corporation.
"The markets tend to be less responsive to bullish factors than to bearish factors, as investors shift into more volatile commodities such as grains and precious metals," Iimori said.
The benchmark August rubber contract on the Tokyo Commodity Exchange (TOCOM) ended Monday's morning session at 156.1 yen per kg, against 155.1 yen last Friday.
Similarly, the benchmark August contract on the Kobe Rubber Exchange was quoted at 156.4 yen in the morning, compared with 155.3 yen last Friday.
Traders say they are also watching the currency market to see if the yen will dip further against the dollar.
Iimori said the upside at 160 yen per kg for the TOCOM benchmark August will be tough to break unless the dollar rises above 125 yen.
The dollar stood at around 123.60 yen in early afternoon trade in Tokyo on Monday.
Despite the yen's weaker tendency, an expected rise in natural rubber stocks in Japan is undermining market sentiment, the traders said.

"There is a view that Japanese rubber stocks will rise again to around 40,000 tonnes as shipments from Thailand may increase from the end of March as a result of active physical buying by trade houses in February," one trader at a major trading house said. "That will help put a lid on further gains in rubber prices here," he said.

Open interest in TOCOM rubber futures fell to 160,000 lots last week, the first time it had fallen to that level since October 1993 as static rubber prices in recent months thinned speculative interest.
The offer price for Thai rubber to Japan on Monday was quoted at $125.50 per kg on a free-on-board basis, little changed from late last week.
In the local physical market, benchmark Thai rubber for large-lot end users was quoted at 169 yen per kg on Monday, against 166 yen on March 10.
